title: When the Gravity Breaks Anew
premise: Edmund Marchetti, a xenolinguist whose dreams have gone silent in every human tongue, ferries cargo along the dead routes between colonies that stopped transmitting years ago. When a passenger manifest lists a name belonging to a ship that was never built, he follows it to Meridian Station, where an entire colony's massacre has been erased from every archive, memory bank, and mind. With a rogue archivist named Sefa Oyelaran and the massacre's sole surviving witness—a child who remembers in a language Edmund alone can still parse—Edmund must reconstruct the truth and broadcast it before Earth's final transmission loop closes forever. In the end, justice arrives not through law but through memory itself: the broadcast succeeds, Earth hears, and Edmund finally dreams again—in the witness's language.
about_author: Mirabel Vane is the pen name of a former shipping-log analyst who spent nine years aboard long-haul freighters before turning to fiction. They write about language, distance, and the people who keep records no one asked them to keep.

chapters.title: The Silent Route
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He runs cargo between colonies that have gone linguistically dark, cataloguing dying languages he can no longer dream in. A routine stop reveals his next manifest contains a name—Vessel Kestrel—that matches no ship ever registered. The beat is quiet unease: a man fluent in dead tongues recognizing one that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: A Name That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Edmund investigates the manifest anomaly at Port Halcyon; station records self-corrupt as he reads them. He meets Sefa Oyelaran, a disgraced archivist who has been tracking similar erasures across three systems. POV alternates. Emotional beat: two lonely professionals realizing they've each seen the same ghost.

chapters.title: Meridian, Population Zero
chapters.summary: They jump to Meridian Station, officially decommissioned and uninhabited for eleven years. Life support is running. Someone is home. Edmund's POV, dread building as familiar colony signage appears in a language he last heard spoken by settlers now listed as never having existed.

chapters.title: The Child Who Remembers
chapters.summary: In the hydroponics bay they find Iyo, a ten-year-old survivor speaking a creole of Meridian settler dialects. She doesn't remember the massacre—but her body does; she flinches at recorded voices. Sefa's POV. Beat: tenderness sharpening into resolve—they are no longer investigating, they are protecting.

chapters.title: Records of Nothing
chapters.summary: Sefa decrypts Meridian's archive core: eleven years of logs replaced with benign agricultural reports so seamless even checksums agree. Edmund realizes the falsification required native fluency in Meridian's own linguistic structure. His POV. Beat: horror—the eraser knew these people intimately.

chapters.title: The Loop
chapters.summary: They discover Earth's last transmission loop: a 72-hour repeating broadcast window before the relay network goes permanently dark. Whatever truth they recover must fit inside it. Sefa's POV, ticking-clock tension established alongside grief for a civilization choosing to stop listening.

chapters.title: What the Walls Heard
chapters.summary: Edmund reads the station's acoustic residue—sound absorbed into structural polymer over years. Buried beneath routine noise: gunfire, sealed bulkhead alarms, a lullaby sung over a public address system during the killing. His POV. Beat: the past physically present, undeniable, unbearable.

chapters.title: Passengers of the Kestrel
chapters.summary: The manifest name resolves: Kestrel was the evacuation ship Meridian's council secretly commissioned—and it never launched. Its passenger list is the victim list. Sefa's POV. Beat: the bureaucratic horror of names reduced to a document that officially cannot exist.

chapters.title: Hunters on the Dark Route
chapters.summary: An enforcement vessel, the Cauterant, arrives claiming piracy jurisdiction. Its commander, Deputy Warden Ash Corliss, offers protection that feels like capture. Edmund's POV. Beat: the law arriving not as refuge but as threat—loyalty to institutions begins to curdle.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Corliss interviews Iyo 'for her safety'; Edmund listens through a hidden channel and hears leading questions designed to implant doubt about her memories. Sefa's POV. Beat: protective fury, and the first open fracture between our trio and lawful authority.

chapters.title: The Linguistics of Denial
chapters.summary: Edmund analyzes Corliss's speech patterns and finds rehearsed phrasing identical to the archive falsifiers' style—one author behind both the massacre's cover story and its enforcement. His POV. Beat: cold clarity; this is conspiracy with a grammar.

chapters.title: Iyo Speaks
chapters.summary: Through play and drawing, Iyo begins narrating what she saw in her creole: families marched to the docking ring, told Kestrel had come for them. Sefa translates with Edmund. Her POV rendered through the adults. Beat: devastating innocence—the lie that made the killing painless.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Greenhouse
chapters.summary: A station caretaker droid, reprogrammed by Corliss's team, attempts to take Iyo. Sefa is injured shielding her; they escape into the maintenance spine. Edmund's POV. Beat: fear and guilt—he brought the child into danger by following a name.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Hidden in the reactor log's metadata, Sefa finds the falsification's author signature: a colonial administrator, Davor Rehn, now a celebrated Earth official credited with 'resettling' Meridian. Sefa's POV. Beat: righteous anger with a target—the massacre has a face.

chapters.title: Corliss's Choice
chapters.summary: Edmund confronts Corliss privately, offering the acoustic evidence. Corliss admits she suspected but chose career over conscience—until hearing the lullaby recording. Her POV (a rare shift). Beat: a wavering ally; loyalty vs. truth embodied in one conflicted officer.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: The transmission loop opens. They race to assemble the broadcast: acoustics, the Kestrel manifest, Iyo's testimony, Rehn's signature. The Cauterant locks down the relay tower. Edmund's POV. Beat: breathless momentum, everything converging.

chapters.title: The Language of Witness
chapters.summary: Earth's receivers won't accept unverified colonial data—unless transmitted in a registered language. Only Meridian creole qualifies, and only Edmund can speak it. He must deliver Iyo's testimony in a tongue he hasn't dreamed in since childhood trauma. His POV. Beat: the personal wound becomes the instrument of justice.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax part one: Sefa fights through the relay lockdown while Edmund speaks Iyo's words live, Corliss holding the door against her own officers. The loop carries testimony outward for seventy-two hours whether anyone silences them or not. Multiple POVs interwoven. Beat: sacrifice, defiance, transmission.

chapters.title: Rehn Descends
chapters.summary: Climax part two: Rehn himself arrives with a wipe-team to erase Meridian physically. Confrontation in the archive core where it all began. Iyo, hidden, recites the victims' names aloud in creole—names Rehn cannot bear to hear. His composure breaks on open channels. Beat: evil forced to witness its own record.

chapters.title: After the Loop Closes
chapters.summary: The loop ends. Silence. Then responses arrive from three colonies and a fragment of Earth's judiciary: hearings demanded, Rehn detained by his own security detail after Corliss testifies. Sefa's POV. Beat: exhausted, disbelieving relief—justice outside the law, ratified by it too late but not never.

chapters.title: Kestrel, Finally Launched
chapters.summary: Resolution: the colonists' remains are given a launch ceremony aboard a renamed vessel, Kestrel, their names restored to every registry. Iyo asks Edmund if the dead will hear their own language again. He says yes, and believes it. His POV. Beat: mourning transformed into ceremony.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Creole
chapters.summary: Epilogue. Months later, Edmund and Sefa ferry Iyo toward a new home among descendants of other erased colonies. Edmund dreams for the first time in years—not in any human language he was born to, but in Meridian creole, full of voices. Final beat: memory kept alive is a living thing, and he is its keeper now.
